sections.title: Velocity and momentum
sections.summary: The speed and direction you carry from one movement phase into the next.
sections.practice: Use cl_showpos in a local practice session. Record the speed and direction before a jump, during the air phase and after landing.

body.text: Velocity is a vector. It has a magnitude (speed) and a direction. Horizontal velocity describes travel across the map; vertical velocity describes rising or falling. A speed number alone cannot tell you which way you are travelling. Two attempts can show the same speed while following different paths.

Momentum is the movement you carry into the next phase. A camera turn does not instantly rotate the velocity vector. Ground contact, [[ground-acceleration-friction|friction]], air acceleration, crouch state, ramps and collision normals can all change it. That is why you can face backwards while still travelling forwards, or hit a wall at an angle and leave with a different line.

Read the HUD at four points: before takeoff, at the first air strafe, at the fastest point and after landing. `cl_showpos 1` can expose position, velocity and view information in a local practice session. Compare the velocity components when available, not just the rounded speed display.

When you lose distance, find the first phase that differs from a successful attempt. A poor approach changes takeoff speed; a bad first strafe changes the flight path; a late crouch can catch the target edge; a hard landing can apply a speed penalty. The final miss is often only the last symptom.

items: Separate horizontal speed from vertical velocity and facing direction.
Record pre-speed, peak speed, takeoff angle, landing position and post-landing speed.
Keep the map, server mode, start marker and input sequence fixed between trials.
Do not call a camera turn an acceleration event unless the velocity readout changes.

body.text: The developer console command `cl_showpos 1` displays position and [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] information in the game. The exact on-screen layout can change, but the [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] readout is useful for comparing attempts made under the same conditions.

For a fair comparison, use the same weapon, map, server, starting position and route. Note horizontal speed separately from vertical motion where the display provides both. A single peak number does not tell you whether you can control the landing or repeat the result.

If your practice map provides a movement HUD, use it to compare takeoff speed, maximum speed and the speed you carry into the landing. Treat plugin labels as that server’s measurement system, not as Valve’s official terminology.

sections.title: Ground acceleration and friction
sections.summary: Why running builds or preserves speed, and why ground contact can remove it.
sections.practice: Run the same short route three times: straight, diagonal left and diagonal right. Compare the speed and direction at one marked point.

body.text: Ground movement changes speed through acceleration while an input is held and friction when the player is on the ground. Friction acts during contact, so a landing can remove speed even when your camera and keys appear to remain unchanged.

The useful run-up is the one that produces the required takeoff [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] and angle. A straight run is easiest to measure. A diagonal or curved approach can create a better line for a particular jump, but it can also leave you with less speed in the direction of the target.

When testing an approach, compare the speed at the same physical point rather than after a different amount of time. Do not confuse maximum speed with useful speed: a high number aimed away from the landing platform is not a good setup.

A [[counter-strafing|counter-strafe]] is a deliberate opposite-direction input used to cancel ground movement. It is a control technique for stopping or setting up a new line, not a universal acceleration trick.

items: Use a fixed start and measure speed at the same takeoff mark.
Compare straight and diagonal run-ups separately.
Avoid unnecessary key overlaps when changing direction.
Do not infer acceleration from the viewmodel or camera animation alone.

sections.title: Ticks, inputs and subtick
sections.summary: How CS2 records input timing and why old tick-perfect advice can be misleading.
sections.practice: Record a short bhop attempt with an input overlay and compare a clean landing with one where you add a movement-key change just before touchdown.

body.text: CS2 accepts movement input with subtick timing. A button press or release can be represented at a point within a simulation tick, which matters for landings, crouch transitions and other frame-sensitive movement.

A subtick input system does not mean that every mechanical outcome is perfectly continuous or independent of client frame rate. The exact order in which input changes are processed can matter. Community reverse-engineering of CS2 bhopping shows that an extra input close to landing can split a movement step and change whether a hop is treated as perfect or restored.

Valve documented several relevant changes: in September 2025 it improved timestep-independence for subtick movement acceleration; in January 2026 it changed landing-time calculations and the [[bhop|bhop]] acceptance window. Those are reasons to prefer current CS2 demonstrations over copied CS:GO tick counts.
Do not treat “one tick” as a universal answer for CS2 jumpbugs or bhops. Note the build, server rules, framerate range and the actual input sequence when testing a frame-sensitive route.

items: Record the game build and server mode.
Keep frame rate stable during A/B tests.
Change one input timing at a time.
Do not convert a community millisecond measurement into a universal tick recipe.

sections.title: Surfaces and collision
sections.summary: The shape of the world matters as much as your inputs.
sections.practice: Repeat a jump against a flat wall, a rounded edge and a ramp in a practice map.

body.text: Player movement is resolved against map collision geometry. Floors, ramps, walls, ledges and corners can change whether you are grounded, sliding, blocked or airborne. A tiny difference in contact position can produce a different result in a precision movement attempt.

Valve has issued movement-related fixes involving surfing, excessive speed near walls and air-strafe [[velocity-momentum|velocity]]. Those patch notes are a reminder that collision and movement edge cases can change between builds.
For reproducible practice, use the same map version and approach angle. Do not assume two visually similar edges have identical collision shapes.

sections.title: Movement quirks and edge cases
sections.summary: Account for patch-sensitive subtick, wall and collision behaviour when diagnosing odd results.
sections.practice: Run the same line beside a wall and in open space, then compare the velocity trace.

body.text: Small changes in collision, player height, input timing and subtick processing can change a route. These are movement edge cases, not a separate named technique category. The community term “kwerks” does not have a standardised definition in the sources checked, so this guide treats it as “movement quirks”.

Valve fixed an air-strafing [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] issue in July 2025, improved subtick acceleration consistency in September 2025, fixed surfing ramp and air-acceleration issues in November 2025, and fixed excessive speed when moving against walls in August 2026.

When a movement suddenly behaves differently, check the game build, server rules, map update, collision shape and your input sequence. Avoid explaining every unusual acceleration as a secret technique; some are bugs that Valve later fixes.

items: Record the exact map and build.
Repeat the same movement away from walls and edges.
Check whether crouch or jump state changed.
Compare a current recording with the date of the source clip.

sections.title: Common mistakes, small corrections and practice habits
sections.summary: A checklist for making movement attempts repeatable and diagnosing avoidable errors.
sections.practice: In Movement Hub, repeat one jump five times while changing only one variable per attempt.

body.text: A movement attempt contains several linked phases: line-up, approach, takeoff, air control, contact and recovery. A mistake early in the sequence can look like a problem with the final jump. Review the earliest point where your successful and failed attempts begin to differ.

Keep your camera direction and [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] direction separate. A smooth turn can change your view without instantly rotating the movement you already carry. Use the speed and position display to check what happened rather than judging the crosshair alone.

When practising air strafes, avoid adding extra keys out of habit. Learn the movement sequence for the specific drill first, then add forward, backward or crouch inputs only when the route calls for them. See [[air-strafing|air strafing]], [[backwards-air-control|backward air control]] and [[jump-crouch|jump-crouch timing]].

items: Use the same start marker, map, server and movement mode for comparisons.
Change only one thing at a time: run-up, takeoff point, mouse arc, crouch or jump timing.
Record a full attempt, including the setup and landing.
Do not compare attempts made with different movement rules or server settings.
Check patch dates when an old route behaves differently.
Use a current clip with a visible keyboard overlay before copying a precise route.

sections.title: Basic directional movement
sections.summary: W, A, S and D create a desired movement direction relative to your view.
sections.practice: Walk a square route using only one direction input at a time, then combine directions.

body.text: W moves toward the direction you face, S moves away, and A/D move sideways relative to your view. Combining keys creates diagonal movement. The direction you look and the direction you travel are related, but they are not the same thing once you have [[velocity-momentum|momentum]].

When you rotate your view while moving, your existing [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] does not instantly rotate with it. You can therefore face one way while carrying speed in another direction. This distinction becomes central to [[air-strafing|air strafing]] and backward movement.
Use simple routes first. Make one controlled turn, watch how your path changes, then add a second turn. Avoid holding every direction key while trying to understand a single mechanic.

Test diagonal movement with W+A and W+D.
Use A/D for side movement relative to your current view, not relative to the map.

sections.title: Counter-strafing
sections.summary: Tap the opposite direction to stop before firing.
sections.practice: Move right, tap left briefly, and fire only when your player has stopped.

body.text: Counter-strafing means applying an opposite movement input to cancel existing ground [[velocity-momentum|velocity]]. If you are moving right with D, a brief A input accelerates you back toward a stop. Reverse the inputs when moving left.
The goal is not to run in the opposite direction. A short tap is enough when timed correctly; holding the opposite key too long makes you accelerate away from the stop and begin moving the other way.
Counter-strafing is a ground shooting skill. Do not use the same idea blindly during a [[long-jump|long jump]], where reversing your input can change the flight path you are trying to preserve.

items: Moving right: tap A to brake.
Moving left: tap D to brake.
Watch for the moment your [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] reaches zero before firing.
If you move the other way, shorten the tap rather than pressing harder.

sections.title: Crouch and duck input
sections.summary: Crouch changes player posture and can affect jump clearance and timing.
sections.practice: Compare a normal jump, a crouch jump and a jump with crouch released before landing.

body.text: Crouching changes the player’s collision posture and the position of the model. A [[crouch-jump|crouch jump]] is useful for clearing geometry that a normal jump cannot reach, but the order and timing of jump and crouch inputs matter.

Do not assume every short crouch tap creates a mini-jump in current CS2. Older Source and CS:GO movement references describe duck-tap and double-duck behaviours, but those exact timings can depend on the build, game mode and server modifications.

For ordinary ledge clearance, start with a straightforward jump followed by crouch while airborne. Then test release timing separately. Avoid mixing crouch-jump experiments with [[bhop|bhop]] or [[jumpbug-vanilla|jumpbug]] drills until you can identify each input’s effect.

Change only the crouch timing between attempts.

sections.title: Approach setup and takeoff line
sections.summary: Prepare a route with a repeatable run-up, direction and takeoff point.
sections.practice: Mark a run-up on a flat surface and repeat the same jump from the same takeoff point.

body.text: A route begins before the jump input. Your approach determines the horizontal [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] and direction that you carry into the air. A clean takeoff from a consistent point is easier to improve than a fast run-up that changes every attempt.

Pick a visible floor seam or map mark. Start from the same spot, move toward the edge and avoid last-second steering unless the route specifically needs it. Make the takeoff direction match the target rather than simply facing it with the camera.
Use [[velocity-momentum|[[velocity-momentum|velocity]]]] to compare attempts. If two jumps have different pre-speeds or different approach angles, they are not controlled comparisons.

Keep the same movement keys during the run-up.
Record the takeoff position and horizontal speed.
Change only the run-up length or steering angle when testing.

Keep the view and route fixed while you test. Make one short diagonal movement, then compare it with a straight run and with an opposite-direction correction.

sections.title: Air strafing
sections.summary: Steer and accelerate while airborne with a side key and matching mouse movement.
sections.practice: In Movement Hub, jump across a wide open area. Release W, perform A-left then D-right, and try to land on a marked line.

body.text: Air strafing lets you steer and build horizontal speed while airborne. The standard learning drill is: jump, release W, hold A while moving the mouse left, then release A and hold D while moving the mouse right. Keep the key and mouse direction matched during each phase.

The key controls the desired side acceleration; mouse movement changes the view-relative direction used by the air-movement calculation. Turning the mouse without the matching side key is not the same strafe. Holding A while turning right usually produces a poor or opposing input for the intended left strafe.

Start with broad, smooth arcs. A flick can turn your view faster than your [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] can respond and may throw the landing line away. As you improve, shorten the arcs and change direction earlier. A successful strafe adds useful velocity while preserving the line toward the target.

Forward input (W) is useful during the approach, but many long-jump drills release W at takeoff so the A/D strafes can shape the air path cleanly. Backward-facing movement and S-input drills need their own practice because view direction and travel direction are not the same thing.

Every route has a different time budget. A short hop may need one controlled strafe; a long airborne route may need several. More strafes do not guarantee more speed. Each reversal costs time and can send you away from the target.

sections.title: Strafe sync and mouse control
sections.summary: A good strafe keeps the directional input and mouse turn working together.
sections.practice: Record three attempts on the same jump: one smooth, one with rushed reversals and one with fewer, longer strafes. Compare each stat rather than choosing by appearance alone.

body.text: Sync is a movement-HUD or [[reading-jumpstats|jumpstats]] measurement of how often the mouse turn and the selected A/D input line up with a useful acceleration direction. Different plugins can calculate or display it differently, so compare scores from the same tool and mode.

A high sync value is useful, but it is not a complete jump score. Takeoff speed, first-strafe timing, path curvature, strafe width, dead air, landing offset and the number of reversals all matter. A high-sync jump can still miss if the whole arc points away from the target.

Use the sync readout to identify a specific phase. If the first strafe scores well and the second does not, check the transition: release the first side key, reverse the mouse smoothly and press the other side key. Do not hold both keys while you are trying to reverse.

“Dead strafe” appears in community discussion as shorthand for a longer held strafe phase, often described around a jump’s second strafe. It is not a formal CS2 movement mode or a universally defined jump type. Treat it as an input-shaping idea and test the exact route, not a rule that the second strafe must always be longer.

sections.title: Alternating left and right strafes
sections.summary: Switch sides smoothly to build a curved path through the air.

body.text: An alternating strafe is a coordinated change from A-left to D-right or from D-right to A-left. Release the old side key as you begin the reverse mouse arc; then press the new side key. Avoid overlapping A and D unless a documented route specifically asks for a special input pattern.

The air path is a curve made from several movement phases. Each strafe changes the [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] vector; your camera can rotate faster than your movement direction changes. If you reverse too late, you keep travelling across the old arc and may run out of room to land.

For a short jump, one left/right pair may be enough. With more airtime, you can use extra reversals to steer around an obstacle or correct your landing. A longer strafe is not automatically wasted, and a higher strafe count is not automatically better. Choose the pattern that produces the required speed and endpoint.

Keep the mouse movement continuous through the reversal. A sharp snap often creates a wide, unstable path. If you reach the edge of your mouse pad, reset your hand during a safe part of the route rather than interrupting the most important correction.

body.text: S requests movement opposite your current view direction. It does not instantly cancel momentum that you already built. If you turn around while moving forward, your view can face the direction you came from while your [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] still carries you ahead.

The correct input depends on the angle between your current [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] and the view direction. Start with small changes so the result is easy to read.

Do not assume S is simply the reverse of W in an air-strafe sequence. W, S, A and D are view-relative; the velocity vector is world-relative. This distinction explains why a backward-looking player can keep moving forward and why a late S press may not stop the existing drift.

body.text: In the air, the player carries existing [[velocity-momentum|velocity]]. Changing your view changes the direction in which the movement keys are interpreted, but the [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] vector still has to be changed through acceleration over time.

body.text: Circle strafing is a way to shape a curved path through the air. You alternate a side key and matching mouse movement so the travel direction bends around an arc rather than following a straight line. Start with a wide circle on open ground. Jump, release W and use A-left followed by D-right. Keep each turn smooth and watch where your [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] carries you. A complete camera circle does not guarantee a complete movement circle because velocity changes more slowly than the view.

For tight routes, use shorter arcs and begin the correction early. A large late correction can pull the player away from the landing. The number of strafes depends on the airtime and path width; the objective is the route, not a target strafe count.

sections.practice: On a long-jump block, compare an even A/D pattern with a longer second phase. Keep the starting speed and target unchanged.

body.text: “Dead strafe” appears in community discussion around high-level movement clips. One explanation describes holding the second strafe longer to gain or preserve a useful [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] component, then using later turns to correct the landing. The term is not a Valve mechanic name and has no single formal CS2 definition.

A longer strafe can be useful when the current [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] and target direction favour one sustained input. It can also be harmful if it bends the route too far or delays the next correction. The result depends on current speed, vertical phase, mouse angle and the route’s landing point.

Treat this as a practical air-control variation, not a trick that every jump should use. Compare the same route with a normal alternating pattern and a longer held second phase. Read the speed trace and landing offset before deciding whether it helped.

items: Use a route with enough airtime for at least two strafes.
Record a normal A/D pattern as the baseline.
Hold the second strafe longer on the next attempt.
Compare Max speed, sync, path and landing position.
Do not assume the second strafe must always be the long one.

body.text: A normal jump is the baseline for every other jump technique. Start with a controlled run, press jump once, and watch how the player rises, reaches the apex and falls back to the ground.

Your takeoff position, horizontal [[velocity-momentum|velocity]], surface and landing height all affect the result. For a fair comparison, practise from a flat surface to a target at the same elevation before adding gaps or sloped ground.
Once the normal jump is repeatable, add one variable: a side strafe, a crouch input, a different takeoff point or a different landing height. This makes it clear what the new input changed.

items: Mark a takeoff point and a landing target.
Practise without crouching first.
Keep the approach speed the same between attempts.

sections.title: Edge jump (EJ): takeoff at the ledge
sections.summary: A jump timed at the final usable ground contact on an edge.

body.text: An edge jump is a takeoff timed close to the end of a platform. The useful skill is controlling the final grounded moment and the direction of the takeoff. It is a route-timing technique, not the same thing as an [[edgebug|[[edgebug|edgebug]]]], which concerns a landing collision.

Approach the edge at a steady speed, keep the intended travel direction, and use a visual marker to repeat the takeoff point. A jump pressed too early wastes part of the platform; a jump pressed after ground contact has ended may become a fall instead.
The exact result depends on the platform collision and the movement state. Do not copy a fixed distance or tick count from a clip recorded on another map or build.

items: Use a visible edge marker and the same run-up.
Keep the camera and movement direction aligned with the target.
Compare early, clean-edge and late attempts.
Do not confuse an edge jump with an [[edgebug|edgebug]] or [[jumpbug-vanilla|jumpbug]].

sections.title: Bunny hop (bhop)
sections.summary: Chain jumps through consecutive landings using controlled air movement and correctly timed jump input.
sections.practice: In Movement Hub, practise single hops first, then add one air strafe and build a short chain.

body.text: A bunny hop chains a jump into the next landing. The basic loop is: jump, control the air path, prepare the next input, then jump again as the player lands. A scroll-wheel bind produces repeated jump presses, which gives you several input opportunities instead of one spacebar tap.

CS2 bhopping is not simply the old CS:GO “first grounded tick” rule. Valve’s 21 January 2026 update says landing time is calculated with subtick precision and that a jump press inside `sv_bhop_time_window`, centred on landing time, can count as a successful bhop if the jump-spam penalty has not rejected it. Valve also made legacy behaviour available for private servers through `sv_legacy_jump`. On 22 January, Valve clarified that landing vertical [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] affects landing speed penalties.

Community reverse-engineering by zer0k-z reports that jump presses that are too close together can be rejected by the jump-spam penalty. Its automated tests suggest a scroll interval around 16 ms performed well in its tested setup. Treat that as a measured starting point, not a Valve recommendation or a guaranteed setting for every server, input device and future build.

The same research found that movement-key changes close to touchdown can affect whether a hop is classified as perfect, restored or delayed. Complete a left/right strafe transition before landing when possible, then make the next jump input the next important event. This is a useful drill, not a universal law for every server configuration.

items: Start with one jump and one landing; do not begin by trying to chain ten hops.
Use a scroll bind only if it gives you repeatable input. It does not guarantee a perfect hop.
Keep your A/D transition smooth and avoid changing several keys at touchdown.
Compare the result on the same server and map. Server settings can change the bhop rules, so record them with the attempt.
Do not use multi-action movement macros on official servers; Valve has restricted certain automated multi-input binds.

sections.title: CS2 bhopping and movement patch history
sections.summary: A dated record of Valve changes that affect movement, bhopping, surfing and collision.

body.text: CS2 bhopping has changed since launch. Old CS:GO tutorials often describe tick-perfect landing rules that no longer match the current default game. Use this timeline when reviewing older clips or config advice.

items: 30 July 2025: Valve fixed a case where movement-button changes could be ignored while turning the view at very high frame rates, and a case where [[air-strafing|air strafing]] produced higher-than-usual [[velocity-momentum|velocity]].
1 August 2025: Valve fixed a [[bhop|bhop]] penalty that could keep accumulating when jump was not pressed, and changed the jump-spam clock to begin when the input registers.
17 September 2025: Valve improved timestep-independence for subtick movement acceleration.
4 November 2025: Valve fixed incorrect air-acceleration clamping while surfing and a ramp-apex identification issue.
21 January 2026: Valve moved landing-time calculation to subtick precision and changed the [[bhop|bhop]] acceptance window. `sv_legacy_jump` can restore legacy behaviour on private servers.
22 January 2026: Valve adjusted landing penalties so landing vertical [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] also affects the result.
24 August 2026: Valve fixed a case where player speed became too high when moving against walls.

body.text: These notes describe fixes and rule changes, not a list of guaranteed movement exploits. For the latest practical explanation of jump timing, read [[bhop|the current bhop section]] and the linked community reverse-engineering study in Sources.

Map geometry changes also matter. For example, Valve extended Inferno A balcony on 4 March 2026 and adjusted nearby clipping. Old route clips may begin or end on geometry that no longer exists in the same position.

sections.title: Crouch jump
sections.summary: Use jump and crouch together to clear geometry that needs a higher effective jump.
sections.practice: On a low box, compare a normal jump, crouch at takeoff, and jump followed by crouch. Record which collision edge changes.

body.text: A crouch jump combines a jump with a crouch input so the player can use a lower collision shape during part of the movement. It is useful for climbing onto geometry, clearing a lip, fitting through a low opening or landing on an elevated edge. The exact height and useful timing depend on the obstacle.

For a simple drill, start a normal jump and add crouch as you leave the ground. Keep crouch held until your head and feet have cleared the relevant geometry. Then compare it with a jump where crouch starts slightly earlier or later. The model animation is not a reliable substitute for checking the collision result.

A crouch jump is not the same as pressing crouch after you have already reached the top of a jump. The latter is an air-crouch or [[jump-crouch|jump-crouch]] sequence. Short clips often use these names loosely, so inspect the actual input order before copying a route.

Do not assume crouch makes every jump higher. It changes the player’s collision shape and clearance; some routes gain access to a ledge because the player can fit under or around geometry. The best test is the exact block or lip you need to reach.

body.text: Air crouch changes the player’s collision bounds while the player is rising or falling. A route can use that smaller shape to pass under an overhang, avoid catching a roof, or place the feet on a narrow surface. The visual model can lag or obscure the exact collision state, so watch the feet and contact point.

Crouch release also matters. In a [[crouchbug-vanilla|crouchbug]], releasing crouch while the ducked feet are close to the floor moves the feet downward. Community reverse-engineering describes a narrow 9–11 unit height range in which this can register an immediate landing. That is a separate, frame-sensitive interaction, not a general-purpose landing trick.

Do not release crouch at a guessed fixed tick. The useful point depends on vertical speed, frame timing, geometry and the current build. Learn ordinary crouch clearance first, then study the dedicated [[crouchbug-vanilla|crouchbug]] and jumpbug sections.

body.text: A long gap jump in ordinary CS2 is a route challenge. It uses the same fundamentals as a normal jump: approach speed, takeoff direction, air control, collision and a landing target. Measure a standard CS2 gap jump by its start point, takeoff speed, flight path and landing point.

Approach from a fixed line, leave the edge with the right horizontal direction, then use measured air strafes to shape the path. The camera should move with the intended strafe, but your [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] will lag behind the camera turn.

Do not treat a distance from another server or ruleset as a universal target. The available run-up, server mode, map collision and landing elevation can change the result. A route is successful when you clear the actual target, not when you match a number from another server.

items: Mark the takeoff and landing points.
Use the longest safe run-up that fits the route.
Keep the [[air-strafing|air-strafe]] sequence smooth.
Watch the landing edge; late corrections can cause a miss.

body.text: Jump-crouch means you start the jump, then add crouch during the air phase. This differs from a crouch-jump where crouch is part of the takeoff. The order matters because the player has already left the ground before the collision shape changes.

Use the sequence when you need to clear one edge and then fit beneath another, or when a route needs you to land on a narrow upper surface. Press crouch after the jump has begun, keep it held through the low-clearance portion, then release only when the route requires a standing landing.

The same move can fail in two opposite ways: crouching too early can stop you clearing the first lip, while crouching too late can make the head collide with an overhang. Treat the two collision points as separate constraints and adjust the press point in small steps.

A squat-jump or instant crouch-jump label in community clips may refer to a different key order. Do not infer a universal 200 ms window from one route tutorial. Use the dedicated map example and test it on the current build.

sections.title: Edgebug
sections.summary: A highly precise collision interaction around an edge; not a normal jump input.
sections.practice: Use an edgebug training map. Find one edge at low speed, then repeat from the same start with a slightly different approach angle.

body.text: An edgebug is a precise collision interaction near a surface edge during a fall. The player contacts a very narrow part of the collision boundary and the expected landing or fall result changes. A successful attempt can avoid the normal fall-damage event while preserving movement that an ordinary landing would interrupt.

The route depends on the edge’s collision mesh, the point of contact, the incoming [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] and the angle of approach. Visual edges are not always identical to their collision edges. A decorative lip may have no useful collision, while a thin-looking face can have a wider collision plane than the model suggests.

Learn with a dedicated edgebug map or a clearly marked training surface. Use slow approaches first to find the contact line, then add speed. Record a side view and a [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] readout; an ordinary landing can look similar if the player survives the fall for another reason.

An edgebug is not the same as a [[jumpbug-vanilla|jumpbug]] or [[crouchbug-vanilla|crouchbug]]. Edgebugging uses an edge collision; the other two use crouch-release timing near the floor. Do not copy a [[jumpbug-vanilla|jumpbug]] crouch sequence into an edgebug attempt.

items: Use a map with a known edgebug surface.
Identify the collision edge, not just the visible model edge.
Keep the drop height and approach angle fixed while learning.
Check that the landing event and fall damage actually changed.
Do not assume every corner or pixel ledge can produce an edgebug.

body.text: Pixel surfing is a community route term for maintaining or redirecting movement along a very small, often sloped collision face. The useful surface may be only a few units wide in the visible map, but the exact collision mesh determines whether a player can ride it.

The setup is a controlled entry angle and [[velocity-momentum|velocity]]. Approach the face so the player contacts the intended side, then use the matching side movement and mouse arc to stay aligned. If you hit the surface head-on, clip the wrong face or arrive too low, you may stop or fall instead of sliding.

Pixel surf is not a separate Valve movement mode and there is no universal pixel coordinate or key recipe. One route can depend on a specific mesh seam, while another uses a ramp-like face. Map updates can change it without changing the movement inputs.
Use a current recording with the collision surface visible. If you are documenting a route, include the exact map version, start point, approach speed, contact face, exit and repeated success rate.

items: Locate the actual collision face before practising.
Start slowly and adjust only the entry angle.
Watch the player’s contact and [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] at the surface.
Do not assume a visible pixel edge behaves like a surf ramp.
Retest after map updates.

body.text: Wall strafing uses movement input and view direction while the player is close to a wall. The wall changes the collision constraint, so the useful path may involve sliding along the face or leaving it at an angle rather than moving through open air.

Start by approaching the wall at a shallow angle and identify which side of the player touches it. Use a side input and controlled mouse movement to keep the contact line. If you press into the wall at a steep angle, you can lose forward progress or end up with a different collision response.

KZ mapping documentation lists wallstrafing as a niche route skill in higher difficulty courses. The exact sequence is map- and mode-dependent; the term does not specify one universal A/D and mouse script.
Keep wall strafing separate from a [[wallbug|wallbug]] or ceiling head-bump. A wall strafe steers along a contact surface; a wallbug or head-bump relies on a particular collision event.

body.text: A run boost uses a teammate’s movement and collision to add height or change the player’s path. The player providing the boost and the player receiving it have different jobs. The route usually depends on the booster’s position, the receiver’s takeoff timing and the collision geometry.

A basic setup places the booster at the required ledge or corner, then has the receiver approach and jump onto or against the booster at the correct moment. The exact sequence varies by map and by the surfaces used. A missed timing can produce a normal collision, a short hop or no boost at all.

Do not confuse a run boost with a [[self-boosts|self-boost]]. A run boost uses another player; a self-boost uses the map’s own geometry and the player’s movement. Record the booster and receiver positions separately when documenting a route.

A head-bump is not automatically a speed boost. The route may save time by shortening the arc or creating a better landing position, but it can also remove useful vertical clearance. Compare the route time and exit [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] to an ordinary jump.

Use small, early corrections. Keep the approach aligned with the centre of the vent, begin the air strafe before the route turns, and avoid large mouse sweeps that point you into the side wall. A crouch may be needed for a low opening or a constrained landing, but it changes the collision shape and should be tested separately.
A vent bhop route may use one hop, several hops or a [[jump-crouch|jump-crouch]] transition. The number of jumps is determined by the vent geometry; the phrase does not define one universal route.

body.text: A self-boost uses map geometry and player movement to reach a position that normally looks like it requires a teammate. Typical ingredients include a [[crouch-jump|crouch jump]], a run-up, a narrow ledge, a barrel, a door handle or a collision edge.

Treat each self-boost as a route, not as one universal mechanic. The start point, first contact, intermediate surface, exit jump and final landing all matter. A spot that works on one map can fail after the mapper adjusts the collision mesh or a Valve update changes the geometry.

Do not mix self-boosts with team run boosts or a jumpbug. If the route uses a [[crouch-jump|crouch jump]], learn that first; if it relies on a bug, identify the exact collision event and keep it separate from the ordinary jump.

Advanced versions combine a 360 turn with a [[bhop|bhop]], a narrow plant or flowerpot landing, or a map-specific route. The landing surface and current game geometry decide whether the route is possible. A famous CS:GO-era attempt on Inferno flowerpots is not evidence that the same trick is a repeatable current CS2 route.

sections.title: Jumpbug: standard CS2 movement technique
sections.summary: A standard-CS2 crouch and landing interaction that needs a current-build route demonstration.
sections.practice: Study the crouchbug first. In an offline movement practice map, record several manual attempts at one fixed fall height and inspect the input timing.

body.text: A jumpbug is a [[crouchbug-vanilla|crouchbug]] combined with a jump input. Community reverse-engineering describes the sequence as an uncrouch while the ducked feet are about 9–11 units above the floor, with jump processed in the same client-frame/subtick movement step. The crouch release moves the feet down and registers contact before the ordinary landing path, then the jump leaves the ground again.

The intended result is a small bounce-like departure that can avoid the normal fall-damage and landing-speed penalty. This is not a standard [[bhop|bhop]]. A normal [[bhop|bunny hop]] chains a jump around a landing window; a jumpbug uses the crouch-release collision sequence as well.

CS2 subtick makes the input extremely sensitive. The useful crouch-release window lasts only a few milliseconds at common fall speeds, and the jump must be processed in the same input step. At higher framerates, frames are shorter and there are more possible input moments; at lower framerates, one frame can be wider than the useful height window. This is why the same route can feel inconsistent.

There is no universal tick number that works for every jump height, framerate, map and build. Practise on a repeatable drop with an input overlay, one manual crouch release and one manual jump press. Do not use an old CS:GO macro as a recipe, and do not use automation on official servers.

items: Start with a repeatable low fall and flat landing.
Hold crouch in the air, then release when the ducked feet reach the narrow floor gap.
Press jump in the same client input step as the crouch release.
Record FPS, server mode, vertical speed and the input overlay.
Expect many failures; do not treat one success as a repeatable competitive route.

sections.title: Crouchbug: the landing interaction
sections.summary: A crouch-release interaction that can register floor contact before the ordinary landing step.

body.text: A crouchbug occurs when you release crouch during a fall while your ducked feet are close enough to the floor. Community reverse-engineering describes the useful height as roughly 9–11 units above the floor: releasing crouch moves the feet down by about 9 units, which can register ground contact immediately.

The crouchbug and [[jumpbug-vanilla|jumpbug]] are related but distinct. A crouchbug is the crouch-release landing event. A jumpbug adds a jump press in the same input step so you leave the floor again. The crouchbug description does not require a jump press.

In the described CS2 behaviour, the early contact happens before the ordinary movement landing step. That can prevent the usual fall-damage and landing-penalty path. The mechanic is extremely timing-sensitive and can depend on the current build, frame rate, fall speed and collision surface.

Learn the event from a side-on recording with visible feet and input overlay. Do not copy a fixed tick count from CS:GO. The CS2 input system processes subtick changes and can make the timing window frame-dependent.

Hold crouch during the fall, then release close to contact.
Check whether the player registers a normal landing or an immediate crouchbug contact.

sections.title: Surf fundamentals
sections.summary: Ride angled surfaces by maintaining contact and shaping your exit velocity.

body.text: Surfing uses sloped collision surfaces to redirect movement while the player remains in contact with a ramp. The main task is to control the side of the player touching the ramp, maintain a stable line and leave the surface with a useful exit [[velocity-momentum|velocity]].

On a left or right ramp, use the side key that keeps the player pressed towards the ramp face while moving the mouse to shape the travel direction. The correct key depends on which side is in contact and the direction of travel. There is no safe “always hold A” or “always hold D” rule.

Start on a wide, shallow ramp. Learn to maintain contact without trying to chain ramps. Then practise the exit: aim for the next surface and use air control only after leaving the current ramp. Too much forward input can fight the sideways contact line; a hard mouse flick can throw you off the ramp.

Valve fixed incorrect surf air-acceleration clamping and a ramp-apex detection issue in November 2025. That is why old Source/CS:GO clips may differ from the current CS2 result. KZ slide ramps and resurfs are related route elements but belong in the dedicated KZ chapter, where server mode and course rules are specified.

Use a smooth contact line and small mouse corrections.
Learn the exit as a separate phase.

body.text: “KZ” is a collection of community climbing modes, not one universal movement ruleset. CS2KZ documents two main modes: Vanilla (VNL), which aims to preserve standard CS2 movement while providing quality-of-life tools, and Classic (CKZ), which changes movement rules to make KZ jumps more consistent and skill-driven.

GOKZ is a separate plugin with its own historical mode definitions. Its old wiki lists Vanilla, SimpleKZ and KZTimer, including different bhop, [[pre-strafe|prestrafe]] and crouch rules. That page was last modified in March 2022 and describes the earlier GOKZ/CS:GO environment, so do not treat its values as current CS2KZ defaults.

Before learning a KZ technique, check the server’s plugin, mode, style, teleports setting, map filter and whether [[reading-jumpstats|jumpstats]] are enabled. A result only compares fairly with another run that used the same rules.

body.text: CS2KZ documentation describes two movement modes. Vanilla (VNL) aims to preserve standard CS2 movement and applies quality-of-life features without changing movement-related settings. A VNL course is the closest KZ environment to practising matchmaking movement.

Classic (CKZ) is a separate movement ruleset intended to make KZ bhopping more consistent and less dependent on random landing outcomes. CS2KZ describes a logarithmic bhop speed formula: speed gains are larger at lower initial speeds and diminish as speed increases. The mode supports techniques such as [[kz-prekeep|pre-keep]] and WAD / “our father” tech that do not apply in the same way to VNL.

A record, jumpstat or route is only comparable when the mode matches. A 240-unit [[long-jump|long jump]] in VNL is not directly comparable with the same number in CKZ or an older GOKZ/KZTimer plugin. Check the server’s mode display and the course filter before you compare times or jumpstats.

Classic documentation and naming can evolve. The current CS2KZ website is the reference for the server’s active mode definition; old GOKZ pages describe Source/CS:GO plugin environments and should be treated as historical context unless the server explicitly says it uses those rules.

body.text: CS2KZ uses courses with filters. A filter combines the movement mode, whether teleports are allowed, the difficulty tier and whether the course counts as ranked. A map can therefore expose more than one version of a course.

A course tier describes the challenge of the whole route. Higher tiers can combine [[pre-strafe|prestrafe]], long jumps, multi-strafing, bhops, slide ramps, resurfs, ladder jumps, wallstrafing and route sequencing. It is not a standalone rating for one trick.

body.text: Jumpbug is a community movement technique built around crouch timing near landing. KZ [[reading-jumpstats|jumpstats]] documentation identifies a jumpbug attempt through crouch release timing and a following perfect [[kz-jumpstat-bh|bhop]]. Other community tutorials describe the timing differently, which is exactly why an exact tick count should not be promised for every CS2 server.

The intended result is to avoid an ordinary landing state and continue into another jump with less interruption. Whether the attempt succeeds depends on the current movement rules, crouch state, landing geometry and input timing.

Learn the sequence on a repeatable height. Change the crouch-release timing in small increments and use a compatible [[reading-jumpstats|jumpstats]] plugin if available. Do not rely on an old tutorial’s fixed tick count unless its author tested the same CS2 build and server mode.

sections.title: Slide ramps

body.text: CS2KZ mapping documentation lists slide ramps as a course element. A slide route uses an angled surface to shape the player’s path and preserve or redirect movement through contact with the ramp.

The important phases are the approach, the initial contact, the line along the ramp and the exit. Entering too high, too low or at the wrong angle can change the contact state and make the player leave the surface before the intended point.
A slide ramp may be followed by a jump, a second ramp or a [[kz-resurf|resurf]]. Follow the map’s route markers and avoid assuming that every [[surf-basics|surf]]-like slope uses the same input rule.

body.text: A resurf is a KZ/[[surf-basics|surf]] route transition where the player reconnects with a surfable surface after leaving it or passing through an intervening movement phase. CS2KZ mapping descriptions list resurfs among the more advanced route elements.

A successful re-entry depends on matching the ramp’s angle and contact face while carrying a useful [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] direction. If you meet the ramp head-on or at the wrong height, you may collide, lose speed or fail to establish a stable slide.

The word describes a route element, not one universal trick. Map geometry defines the approach and target surface. Use the map author’s line or an uncut demonstration instead of assuming every ramp can be resurfed.

Keep enough room to align with the ramp normal.
Watch the [[velocity-momentum|velocity]] change at re-contact.
Do not copy a resurf path to another ramp with different geometry.

body.text: CJ is an ambiguous abbreviation. In CS2KZ’s Vanilla course tiers, “CJ” refers to crouch-jump knowledge. Legacy Countjump sources also describe double-countjump (DCJ) and multi-countjump (MCJ). Those names belong to specific older server movement and [[reading-jumpstats|jumpstats]] rules. The exact sequence and measurement can depend on the plugin; the abbreviation alone is not enough to identify the mechanic.

When you see CJ in a map guide, ask which server and mode the author means. A VNL tier description that says CJ does not automatically require the old Countjump sequence. A plugin command that lists CJ does not automatically mean a standard [[crouch-jump|crouch jump]].

sections.summary: A long-jump attempt that begins from a standstill rather than a running prestrafe.
sections.practice: On a KZ practice block, perform several standing jumps from the same line and compare the first strafe and distance.

body.text: A standing [[long-jump|long jump]] starts without a run-up. The player begins from rest, jumps and uses the available air control to cover horizontal distance. It is a useful control drill because it removes the moving approach and makes the first air inputs easier to isolate.

sections.title: Reading KZ jumpstats
sections.summary: Understand the pre-speed, max speed, sync, offset and distance values in a KZ jumpstat.
sections.practice: Save three jumpstat attempts on the same block. Identify which measurement changes first when you improve one input phase.

body.text: Jumpstats turn a jump into a set of measurements. The exact fields depend on the plugin and server mode, so read the HUD legend before comparing attempts. GOKZ documentation gives a useful legacy vocabulary, but its values and jump classifications were designed for its own plugin environment.

`Pre` is the speed at takeoff or ladder exit; `Max` is the highest speed during the jump; `Distance` is the measured horizontal jump distance; `Block` describes the gap or block context; `Edge` and `Deviation` describe where the jump begins and how it crosses the blocks. These values help distinguish a weak approach from a poor air path.

`Strafes` counts the movement turns or mouse-derived phases the plugin detects. `Sync` measures useful alignment between the mouse turn and A/D input. `OL` can show overlap between opposing keys; `DA` can show time with neither side key. `Width` describes the turn amount; `W release` and `Crouch release` compare release timing with the plugin’s expected reference.

`Height`, `Airtime` and `Offset` describe the jump’s vertical arc and the difference between start and landing surfaces. For a block jump, ladder jump or [[jumpbug-vanilla|jumpbug]], the plugin may add specialized fields. Do not assume every HUD uses the same units, offsets or success rules.

Use stats to diagnose one phase at a time. Low Pre points to the approach; a good Pre but low Max may point to air input; good speed but a miss points to path or landing. Compare repeated attempts from the same start in the same mode.

Use Strafes, Sync, OL and DA to review air input.
Use Height, Airtime and Offset to understand the jump arc.
Do not compare legacy GOKZ values with a different CS2KZ plugin as if they share one formula.

body.text: A [[reading-jumpstats|jumpstats]] display can report how many strafes it detected, how well those strafes synced and how much time was spent overlapping or not holding a side key. The calculation is plugin-specific. In older GOKZ documentation, the number of strafes is calculated from mouse movement rather than a raw count of key presses.

Sync should describe useful acceleration, not simply fast mouse movement. A large turn can produce a low-value phase if the matching side key is wrong or if the player is already travelling at an angle that makes the turn unhelpful.

Strafe width describes how far the player turns during a phase. Wider turns are not always better: at higher speed, an excessive arc can bend the route away from the target. Dead air and overlap can expose poor transitions, but a non-zero value is not automatically a failure on every plugin or route.
Use the measurements to fix one issue: reduce overlap, improve the transition, adjust strafe width, or align the landing. Do not chase 100% sync if that makes the jump shorter or less repeatable.
